hook.text: We've found small ones and giant ones, but black holes in the middle range—100 to 100,000 solar masses—are elusive.

buildup.text: Intermediate-mass black holes could be the missing link explaining how supermassive ones grow so large.

discovery.text: In 2020, LIGO detected a 142-solar-mass black hole formed from a merger—the first confirmed intermediate-mass black hole.

twist.text: Some may hide in the centers of globular clusters—dense star swarms where collisions and mergers are frequent.

climax.text: HLX-1, a bright X-ray source in a distant galaxy, may be a 20,000-solar-mass intermediate black hole feeding on gas.

punchline.text: The missing middle child. We know they exist. Finding them is the hard part.

quiz.question: Why are intermediate-mass black holes important for understanding supermassive ones?
options: They may be the building blocks that merged to create supermassive black holes
They emit unique radiation that reveals how all black holes form
They are the only black holes that can be directly photographed

details.summary: Intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) — 100 to 100,000 solar masses — are the missing link between stellar-mass and supermassive black holes. Long theorized, they've been difficult to confirm. Potential candidates include ultraluminous X-ray sources and objects detected via gravitational waves.
details.whyItMatters: IMBHs may explain how supermassive black holes grew so large. Finding them would fill a crucial gap in our understanding of black hole growth and provide clues about galaxy evolution.
takeaways: They bridge stellar-mass and supermassive black holes
Confirming their existence remains an active challenge

faq.question: Where might intermediate-mass black holes be found?
faq.answer: Likely in the centers of globular star clusters, in dwarf galaxies, or wandering through larger galaxies after mergers. Gravitational wave event GW190521 detected a ~150 solar mass remnant, placing it in the intermediate-mass range — the most convincing detection to date.

faq.question: Why are they so hard to detect?
faq.answer: They're too small to dominate galactic dynamics like supermassive black holes and too rare to produce abundant X-ray binaries like stellar-mass ones. Without nearby matter to accrete, they're essentially invisible. Detection requires fortunate circumstances or gravitational wave observation.
